items.title: September 2026 CPI: Inflation Hits 3.7% in a Tough Print for Housing
items.description: Affordability , Data , Economic Coverage , Housing Finance , Market Outlook September 2026 CPI: Inflation Hits 3.7% in a Tough Print for Housing By Jake Krimmel Oct 14, 2026 September’s consumer price index came in hotter than forecasters expected. Headline inflation rose to 3.7% year over year, and core, which had been cooling since May, ticked back up to 2.6%. The 10-year Treasury yield jumped 11 basis points within 15 minutes of the release, a sign that markets are reading this report as a preview of what’s to come. That matters for mortgage rates, which have already climbed 74 basis points since late August. Here’s what today’s report means for the Fed, consumers, and the housing market. September 2026 CPI at a Glance Headline CPI: +0.6% MoM Seasonally Adjusted (SA), following August’s +0.4% rise, versus forecasts of +0.5%; annual rate rose to 3.7% , up from 3.4% in August and above the 3.6% forecast Core CPI (less food energy): +0.3% MoM (SA), matching August; annual rate rose to 2.6% , up from 2.4% in August after falling from 2.9% in May Gasoline: +9.1% MoM (SA), +34.2% YoY, accounting for over half of the month’s total increase Shelter: +0.4% MoM (SA) after +0.3% in August, with rent up 0.2% and owners’ equivalent rent up 0.3%; +3.2% YoY Mortgage rates: Freddie Mac’s 30-year rate stood at 7.4% as of last week, up 74 basis points from 6.66% in late August Market reaction: the 10-year Treasury yield rose 5 basis points immediately after the release and 11 basis points within the first 15 minutes September CPI: hotter than expected, and core is no longer cooling Today’s September Consumer Price Index report came in slightly hotter than expected, with overall inflation at 0.6% month over month and 3.7% year over year, compared to forecasts of 0.5% and 3.6%. Gasoline prices jumped 9.1% in the month, accounting for over half of the monthly increase. Core inflation, which strips out food and energy, also surprised to the upside, rising 0.3% month over month and up 2.6% year over year from 2.4% in August. The uptick in core, which had been trending down from 2.9% in May, is more worrying. Some CPI reports seem backward looking and stale, while others seem like they’re foreshadowing what’s to come. This one definitely feels like the latter. We are in ‘when’ not ‘if’ territory when it comes to the next Fed rate increase. What it means for the Fed: a hike is a matter of when, not if Still, today’s firmer numbers are probably not enough to change the Fed’s holding bias in October, especially given the dovish talk from New York Fed President John Williams earlier this week . But a hold is hardly the slam dunk it was earlier. Today’s numbers all but guarantee a hike by December though, while further opening the door for one or more hikes in early 2027. We are in ‘when’ not ‘if’ territory when it comes to the next Fed rate increase. Bond markets noticed too, with the 10-year Treasury yield up 5 basis points immediately and 11 basis points in the first 15 minutes after the release. The evolution of bond yields and hike odds are two key things to monitor for mortgage rates this week and next. What it means for housing, and homebuyers and sellers This is a tough print for housing, not because of what higher inflation means for right now but because of what it may mean moving forward. Freddie Mac mortgage rates went from 6.66% in late August to 7.4% as of last week , a 74 basis point rise that is good for a 7.2% loss of purchasing power, or over $22,000 in house price for a buyer with a $2,000 monthly principal and interest budget. Given these numbers, it’s no surprise that housing demand has been hit hard. NAR existing home sales fell 2.2% year over year in September, while Realtor.com data show pending sales down 4.1% and new contract signings down 9.8%, both leading indicators for where closed sales are headed in the coming months. items.title: Why falling housing inventory is sending sellers the wrong signal
items.description: The number of homes for sale is beginning to decline as the housing market moves deeper into its seasonal slowdown. But beneath that familiar pattern, buyer demand is weakening, price reductions remain elevated and some sellers are taking their homes off the market. The result is a housing market where falling inventory doesn’t necessarily signal improving conditions for sellers. According to HousingWire Data, national active inventory fell 0.4% during the week ending Oct. 9, reaching 898,139 single-family homes. Inventory remained 4.8% higher than the comparable week in 2025, but the more revealing shift was in buyer activity. New pending sales fell to 54,060, down 15.4% from 63,883 during the equivalent week last year. Meanwhile, 42.89% of active listings had experienced a price reduction, compared with 41.84% one year earlier. Mortgage rates provide an important part of the explanation. In his latest Housing Market Tracker , HousingWire Lead Analyst Logan Mohtashami reported mortgage rates at 7.48%, with the 10-year Treasury yield holding near a critical 5.35% level. Mortgage spreads also widened to 2.12%, adding another layer of uncertainty to the rate outlook. Mohtashami has consistently identified 6.64% as an important mortgage-rate threshold for housing demand. With rates now substantially above that level, purchase applications and pending sales have weakened. But the impact isn’t uniform across housing markets. A closer look at Dallas-Fort Worth, Denver and San Francisco reveals three different relationships between inventory, buyer activity and pricing pressure. Those differences matter for housing professionals trying to understand whether their local market is becoming more competitive, offering buyers greater negotiating leverage or simply experiencing less activity on both sides of a transaction. Dallas shows why falling inventory can be misleading Dallas-Fort Worth offers one of the clearest examples of the disconnect between inventory and demand. Active inventory declined 3.3% between July 17 and Oct. 9, falling from 31,296 to 30,269 single-family homes. On its own, that decline could suggest a tightening market. But pending-sales activity tells a different story. Weekly new pending sales fell 32% during the same period, from 2,026 to 1,378. The comparison with 2025 is particularly revealing. During the week ending July 17, Dallas recorded 2.8% more new pending sales than the equivalent week in 2025. By Oct. 9, that relationship had reversed. New pending sales were 25.7% below the comparable week one year earlier. In just 12 weeks, Dallas moved from slightly outperforming last year’s pending-sales activity to substantially underperforming it. At the same time, pricing pressure remained persistent. Approximately 52% of active listings had experienced a price reduction, and the median list price declined from $450,000 in July to $435,000 in October. Seller withdrawals also increased. During the week ending Oct. 9, 1,390 listings were withdrawn, compared with 724 the previous week. That increase coincided with a weekly inventory decline of 500 homes. However, withdrawals are only one component of changing inventory levels, and the available data does not establish how much of the decline they explain. The broader picture is more important. Fewer homes are available than in July, but substantially fewer buyers are moving into contract. For real estate professionals, that distinction changes how inventory trends should be interpreted. A declining supply of homes does not automatically translate into greater pricing power when buyer activity is falling at the same time. Denver’s growing inventory comes with persistent pricing pressure Denver illustrates a different market dynamic. Active inventory increased 11.4% between July 17 and Oct. 9, rising from 8,166 to 9,100 single-family homes. Over that same period, weekly new pending sales declined 9.1%, from 607 to 552. items.title: GSEs seek to support lenders with efficiencies as rates rise
items.description: Secondary markets GSEs seek to support lenders with efficiencies as rates rise By Bonnie Sinnock CloseText About Bonnie twitter bcynic mailto bonnie.sinnock@arizent.com linkedin bonnie-sinnock-115a829 Published October 14, 2026, 5:52 p.m. EDT | Updated October 14, 2026, 7:09 p.m. EDT 3 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Processing Content Key Insight: Discover how Fannie Mae plans to offset its newly slashed mortgage origination forecast. What's at Stake: Mortgage lenders fighting to maintain revenue as Fannie Mae slashes its volume forecast. Forward Look: Freddie Mac has an ongoing limited engagement called LPA Express. Overview bullets generated by AI with editorial review. Fannie Mae has downshifted its origination forecast for next year but both it and Freddie Mac seek to offset this by offering lenders operational efficiencies they can use to augment capital markets revenue Fannie's reduced projections follows others like the Mortgage Bankers Association that have responded to a rise in rates with less optimistic forecasts for next year. The GSE previously anticipated originations could grow to nearly $2.3 trillion in 2027, but now sees volume falling to below $1.9 trillion. There's still a chance rate environment could improve for lenders next year, but so far, the latest economic indicators have not been promising from that perspective. Given that outlook, the two government-sponsored enterprise loan-buyers told lenders at a recent industry conference that they are working to help mortgage companies serve more borrowers and operate more efficiently while managing rate-related risks. What the GSEs are doing: By the numbers "We are doing business with 30% more sellers than we were four years ago," Sonu Mittal, executive vice president and head of single-family acquisitions at Freddie Mac, told attendees at the MBA's annual meeting in Chicago. Jake Williamson, Fannie Mae's executive vice president and head of single-family, said the GSE is being more nuanced in its underwriting. Fannie Mae is hearing pretty loud and clear from its customers the market is very challenging, so it will get creative about products and policy. "There's not a one-size-fits-all when it comes to risk management. Can we get more granular in the way we approach things? A lot of our investments are really focused on that customer feedback," he said. Mittal said Freddie is working on doing more to work with non-W2 borrowers. "We got a lot of feedback from the industry that not all the jobs are 9-5 anymore," he said. "There is a lot of variable income, which we see in the industry. So we partnered with the industry on fluctuating income in other areas, and we launched the income calculator, which continues to help lenders make sure that they can get the borrowers from point A to point B." He also said Freddie has an ongoing limited engagement called LPA Express. "What we are doing there is validating the income for the lender, and it's showing really, really good promise early on," Mittal said. Both GSEs also touted savings from home valuation options. Fannie has bought around 5.4 million loans using appraisal alternatives , which had produced around $3 billion in savings as of midyear 2026, Williamson said. Mittal said Freddie also is approaching $3 billion in savings for borrowers. "And while we are doing those appraisal waivers, we are continuing to see the quality remain in a really good place, so it's not compromising safety and soundness," he said. Both GSE executives also reported savings from title alternatives. Fannie Mae reported that about 8,000 loans have come in the door on attorney opinion letters with no title defects. Another 22,000 have come in the door through its title acceptance program with no title defects. "The cost savings of just those two things in the last year and a half has been about $25 million. items.title: Russell Galbut Axes 3 Miami Beach Live Local Act Projects
items.description: Russell Galbut Axes 3 Miami Beach Live Local Act Projects October 14, 2026 | 7:39 pm ET Chloe Gallivan, South Florida Miami-based developer Russell Galbut has called it quits on three Miami Beach Live Local Act projects after years of pushback against the legislation from the city and residents. Bisnow/Chloe Gallivan Russell Galbut speaks at the Broward State of the Market event. The developer, who leads GFO Investments and Crescent Heights , wrote an email Monday to Miami Beach City Manager Eric Carpenter, Miami Beach Commissioner Alex Fernandez and Miami-Dade County Commissioner Vicki Lopez, notifying them he was pulling the applications for the projects. Galbut scrapped plans for a 43-story tower with 163 units, 72 of which would be workforce housing, at 1575 Alton Road. He proposed the project in 2024 and was hit with denials through 2026. He has also pulled his plans for a 28-story, 99-unit building that would include 40 workforce housing units at 740 Alton Road and a 28-story, 100-unit project at 880 71st St., which was proposed in partnership with Miami Beach-based Lefferts. "This decision reflects my commitment to collaboration, not my retreat from the need for more housing," Galbut wrote in the email, which was shared with Bisnow. "I believe we can work together to create a Miami Beach approach that encourages responsible investment, protects our neighborhoods, and provides housing for the people who make this city special. And will continue to strive for this always." The Real Deal first reported Galbut's decision to back away from the projects. The Florida Legislature passed the Live Local Act in 2023 to incentivize more affordable and workforce housing development by offering tax exemptions and density and height boosts if developers dedicate at least 40% of a project's units to households making between 80% and 120% of the area median income. Galbut was among the many developers to leverage the Live Local Act when the law was passed. By January 2025, Galbut had proposed six projects in Miami Beach alone. But the city has openly resisted the legislation and the proposed skyscrapers that followed, citing fear that they would threaten the city's historic charm. "If you want to destroy Miami Beach, you want to destroy our tourism-based economy, you want to stop Miami Beach being a destination to the wealthiest people in the world, line up Alton Road with 400-foot towers," Fernandez said at a Bisnow event last year . The law was amended again in 2025 to remove loopholes that cities had been erecting to block qualified Live Local applications, which are supposed to receive administrative approval rather than votes from elected officials or boards. Critics said the changes largely stripped municipalities of say over land use decisions. Following the most recent changes, Miami Beach approved its first handful of projects this year. Galbut, a longtime Miami Beach resident, landed approvals for a 16-story, 204-foot tower at 663 Alton Road in June and, in September , got the go-ahead for a 15-story tower with 29 residential units and office space at 1826 Collins Ave., which he is developing with Lefferts. Galbut's Crescent Heights also revised plans for a 39-story tower at 824 Alton Road with 149 residences split between 72 workforce housing units and 77 market-rate units, Florida YIMBY reported earlier this month. It is unclear if Galbut, who didn't immediately respond to a request for comment, has any new plans for the sites. "I have always believed in the original intent of the Live Local Act: creating much-needed affordable and workforce housing," Galbut wrote in the email. "But I also recognize that the conversation surrounding this legislation has moved away from that intention, and I understand the concerns residents have raised about its impact on our community." items.title: Chicago Office Tower Sells For $550M To Zara Founder In Blockbuster Deal
items.description: Chicago Office Tower Sells For $550M To Zara Founder In Blockbuster Deal October 14, 2026 | 6:23 pm ET Ryan Wangman, Chicago Amancio Ortega , the founder of the fashion retailer Zara , reportedly acquired the 51-story office tower at 1 N. Wacker Drive for about $550M, one of the priciest office deals in the country this year. Wikimedia Commons/TastyPoutine 1 N. Wacker Drive in Chicago Irvine Co . sold the more than 1.4M SF office property to Ortega's family office in a deal Tuesday that includes the assumption of a $353M CMBS loan Irvine took out in 2021, CoStar News first reported . The sale hadn't been posted in Cook County property records as of Wednesday evening. Only two larger full-building office trades occurred nationwide in 2026: the $730M sale of Park Avenue Tower in New York City, which closed in January, and the $691M sale of the Transamerica Pyramid in San Francisco in April. In Chicago, the deal is the largest outright office sale since the Aon Center sold for $712M in 2015. It is the highest valuation since 100% of the equity interest in the Bank of America Tower sold for $210M in March 2022, a deal that put the tower's implied value at more than $1B. The 51-story tower at 1 N. Wacker was completed in 2001 and is about 94% leased to a tenant roster that includes PwC , UBS and Fitch Ratings , according to CoStar. Ortega's real estate investment arm, Ponte Gadea, is no stranger to the city, making another major splash in Chicago when it dropped almost $232M on the 492-unit apartment tower at 727 W. Madison St. in 2023. This is the first time Irvine Co. has exited a Chicago property, CoStar reported. It still owns two other trophy office towers in the city: 71 S. Wacker Drive and 300 N. LaSalle St. The deal for 1 N. Wacker has been in the works for months, with Irvine Co. reportedly beginning to shop the property as early as January. Cushman Wakefield Managing Director Jeff Skender said at last month's Bisnow Chicago lease conference that he was interested in a 1 N. Wacker sale because the property has top-of-the-market rates and minimal vacancy. "The question to owners is: OK, you're trying this hard to maintain your face rates. What is the reward in this capital markets environment on that reversion when you bring that to market?" Skender said at the end of September. "And I think 1 N. Wacker is going to be a really good test of that." items.title: Regulators Reject Proposed Rules For Data Centers On Nation's Largest Grid
items.description: Regulators Reject Proposed Rules For Data Centers On Nation's Largest Grid October 14, 2026 | 6:49 pm ET Dan Rabb, Data Centers Two months after PJM Interconnection proposed a plan that would have fundamentally changed data center development within the largest U.S. power grid, federal regulators have sent it back to the drawing board. Unsplash/American Public Power Association Late last week, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission rejected most of PJM's proposed framework for connecting data centers to its grid system, which spans 13 states across the Mid-Atlantic and Midwest, plus Washington, D.C. PJM has been scrambling to contend with an unprecedented, data center-driven wave of electricity demand that has threatened the grid’s stability and raised customer utility bills. FERC’s ruling means the grid operator must scrap several measures at the heart of its proposed solution, sending PJM back to the drawing board and prolonging uncertainty for developers navigating the regulatory landscape in some of the industry’s most important data center markets. The now-rejected framework PJM submitted to FERC in August would have imposed what amounted to a bring-your-own-capacity requirement on new data centers looking to connect to the grid. New facilities built without adding new generation or other capacity would have faced curtailment during periods when demand for power came dangerously close to exceeding supply. The proposal would have required utilities to cut power to data centers before any action that could disrupt service for residential and commercial customers. It would also have barred these new data centers from participation in a critical power auction that has been responsible for driving up utility bills throughout the PJM system. In its decision to reject these measures, FERC argued that PJM’s proposal overstepped its authority by intruding on retail electricity policies reserved for states under the Federal Power Act. Commissioners also said the proposed rules would have unfairly discriminated against data centers and other large-load customers beyond what is necessary to maintain grid reliability. “We need state regulators to establish clear rules for which customers should be curtailed first when circumstances require it,” FERC Commissioner David Rosner wrote in a concurring opinion issued with the FERC ruling. “And we need PJM to be ready to adjust their operations to this evolving paradigm. But such measures should only be taken when necessary to keep the system reliable, after voluntary demand response resources have been exhausted.” The rejection comes as PJM is warning of mounting reliability risks due to surging electricity demand, much of it from data centers. On Monday, PJM issued a “maximum generation alert” as unusually warm fall weather pushed the system close to its limits. This prompted the Department of Energy to authorize emergency measures that could require some data centers to temporarily run on their on-site backup generation to help avoid a blackout. PJM emphasized that this step is precautionary and that it is unlikely such curtailment measures will be needed. Still, PJM has had several previous close calls, including a near regional blackout when multiple data centers simultaneously disconnected from the grid. Data centers are also driving up electricity costs for consumers, with the price of power set to jump more than 60% in PJM's service area. Following FERC’s ruling, PJM spokesperson Jeff Shields wrote in a statement that the grid operator is “reviewing the Commission’s order with an eye toward how we can fulfill FERC’s requirements while recognizing the responsibilities FERC indicated belong to the states and honoring the concept that existing electricity customers should not be unfairly burdened by new, energy intensive customers in the form of higher costs or decreased reliability.” FERC’s decision is a headache for the tech companies, data center developers and power

items.description: More Details Emerge On Grady's $1B South Fulton Hospital Plan October 14, 2026 | 5:30 pm ET Jarred Schenke, Atlanta New details have come out on Grady Health System ’s planned $1B medical campus south of Downtown Atlanta. Union City , one of the fastest-growing suburban cities in Fulton County, this week filed a development of regional impact permit for the project with Georgia’s community affairs department. The application marks the latest step in the process for Grady to open a new 200-bed acute care hospital along Campbellton Fairburn Road. Google Maps The DRI application states that Grady is seeking to build a 1.1M SF hospital, a 220K SF medical office building and an 18K SF central energy plant on the 40-acre parcel. The campus, once it’s completed by 2036, is expected to contribute $3.6M to $6.8M in local taxes annually and employ 1,880 people full time, according to the application . The Georgia Department of Community Affairs regularly reviews construction projects that will have a regional impact on infrastructure. Grady opened a freestanding emergency room facility at the site in June, which is slated to be integrated into the new hospital. City planners hope the new hospital will address the healthcare desert left by the closures of Wellstar Health System ’s Atlanta Medical Center South and Atlanta Medical Center in 2022. Grady did not respond to a request for comment. The healthcare system first unveiled its medical campus plan in March. The Atlanta Journal-Constitution previously reported that the facility will include a surgery center and a pediatric care unit run by Children’s Healthcare of Atlanta. Grady obtained certificate-of-need approval from the Georgia Department of Community Health in August, a process that ensures there is a need for a new medical facility without duplicating services in a local community, the Atlanta Business Chronicle reported . Fulton County approved $300M in bond funding for the project in March. Grady is planning to pay another $300M and is seeking to raise an additional $300M from philanthropic sources. Grady isn’t the only health system looking to expand into the southern part of Fulton County to address a shortage of acute medical care. Bisnow/Jarred Schenke CPL Architects and Engineers' Douglas Spies, Piedmont Healthcare's Keishia Niblack, McCarthy Building Co.'s Kyle Orr, Atrium Health's Bennett Thompson and Bisnow's Brandon Elsasser In August, Atrium Health , along with Morehouse School of Medicine, obtained approval for a $700M teaching hospital off 675 Metropolitan Parkway, serving Central and South Fulton County communities. Atrium’s goal is “care for all,” with plans to balance redeveloping aged hospitals in its system as well as expanding ambulatory care, Bennett Thompson, the company’s vice president of real estate, said Wednesday during Bisnow ’s Atlanta Healthcare Conference. Atrium, which operates Navicent The Medical Center in Macon and the Floyd Medical Center in Rome, saw an opportunity to expand into South Fulton after the closures of Wellstar’s hospitals, Thompson said. “It’s really about health equity, and that’s driving a lot of it,” he said. “Those are the driving reasons for our investment in Atlanta.” Continue reading this story with a free account Log in or register Contact Jarred Schenke at jarred@bisnow.com Related Topics: Atrium Health , Bennett Thompson , Georgia Department of Community Affairs , Grady Health System , Grady South

items.title: Foreclosure Suit Filed At Stalled Penn Plaza Life Sciences Project
items.description: Foreclosure Suit Filed At Stalled Penn Plaza Life Sciences Project October 14, 2026 | 7:25 pm ET Ciara Long, New York City The new lender to a planned 156K SF lab and office building around the corner from Moynihan Train Hall is trying to wrestle the property from its owner. Google Maps Lenders are pursuing foreclosure proceedings after a planned lab and office building at 320 W. 31st St. never materialized and the borrower allegedly defaulted on a loan. Quinlan Development Group filed a lawsuit Tuesday asking a judge's permission to foreclose on the leasehold interest at 320 W. 31st St., alleging the property's owner defaulted on a $54M mortgage. The property is owned by Maple 1 Farley Owner LLC, an affiliate of Cannon Hill Capital Partners , which planned to build an 11-story building on the site that would combine lab and office space. But the development never took off: The grime-streaked building that once housed part of Touro College’s campus was still standing as of April, according to Google Street View . The total debt owed is now $65.9M, including accrued interest, default interest and additional charges, according to the complaint. Quinlan, which acquired the loan in September from Bank of China , is pushing to schedule a foreclosure auction to satisfy the debt. PincusCo first reported the lawsuit, which was filed in New York County Supreme Court. Cannon Hill is also named as a defendant because it is a recourse guarantor on the mortgage, and Quinlan is reserving the right to go after the development firm if a foreclosure sale doesn't cover the outstanding debt, according to the complaint. Based in Chelsea, Cannon Hill spun out of Columbia Property Trust in 2022 and took over funds Columbia Property acquired when it bought Normandy Real Estate Partners in 2020. Cannon Hill's co-founders, Jeff Gronning and Melissa Cosgrove Donohoe, were executives at Normandy when it was acquired. Columbia Property Trust acquired the ground lease for 320 W. 31st — in the shadow of Facebook's offices at Vornado's renovation of the James A. Farley Post Office — in February 2020 from an entity managed by Onyx Equities for $88M, according to documents filed in the city register. An entity tied to SL Green provided Columbia Property with a $54M loan to finance the purchase, then assigned the debt to Bank of China in June 2021. The loan’s maturity date was later extended to Aug. 18, 2025. But the borrower didn’t pay off the mortgage, leading Bank of China to issue a default notice in September 2025. On Sept. 17 this year, Bank of China assigned its full interest in the loan, mortgages and collateral agreements to an entity controlled by Quinlan. On Tuesday, Quinlan began preforeclosure proceedings. Overtime Properties LLC, registered to Charand Real Estate Associates President Andrew Edelman, has owned the land under the property since 1998, according to city records. Quinlan’s attorneys are seeking the appointment of a receiver to collect rents, manage the property and prevent its value from deteriorating. The property has an open Environmental Control Board violation, Quinlan's attorneys wrote in the filing, claiming “waste and decay” at the property “evidences ongoing mismanagement.” Quinlan, its attorneys, Cannon Hill and Columbia Property Trust didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment. items.title: 2 San Jose Multifamily Towers Change Hands For Combined $380M
items.description: 2 San Jose Multifamily Towers Change Hands For Combined $380M October 14, 2026 | 8:00 pm ET Rob Sabo, San Francisco Bay Area Courtesy of Kennedy Wilson A three-way JV acquired One South Market in downtown San Jose for $176M. Two high-rise apartment buildings in downtown San Jose have traded hands for a total of $380M. A joint venture between Coastal Ridge Real Estate and Brookfield acquired The Grad, a 1,039-bed student housing tower in downtown San Jose, for $204M, while a three-party JV including Kennedy Wilson and Hulic Co. purchased One South Market , a 312-unit tower, for $176M. The Grad, a 19-story Class-A high-rise at 88 E. San Carlos St., is one block from San Jose State University. The 543K SF L-shaped tower was completed in 2020 by developers Amcal and Swenson and has 260 units across 17 floors. It was fully occupied when the sale closed. The sale was promoted after the former owners had trouble refinancing the property amid high interest rates, according to the Silicon Valley Business Journal. The primary investors lacked the capital necessary to obtain refinancing, Swenson CEO Case Swenson told the SVBJ . “If I could hold on to it, I would,” Swenson said. The Grad was refinanced in November 2024 by ACORE Capital Management, which provided a $150M loan to Swenson and Amcal, The Mercury News reported . “The Grad is a modern, Class-A high-rise in the heart of Silicon Valley, a market with deep demand, compressed cap rates and significant barriers to entry,” Institutional Property Advisors Executive Managing Director of Investments Peter Katz said in a press release. Katz represented the selling group, along with Marcus Millichap's Tony Solomon. Kennedy Wilson and Hulic joined up with Fuyo General Lease (USA) Inc. to purchase One South Market. One South Market is a 23-story apartment building completed in 2015. Lakevision Capital sold the property after purchasing it for $175M in 2020. The property's per-unit price of $564K outstrips the five-year average in the area of $467K, the SVBJ reported . “One South Market offers exceptional long-term fundamentals, driven by its prime downtown location, strong employment base and limited new multifamily supply,” Kennedy Wilson Multifamily Division President Kurt Zech said in a statement. “The property provides a unique opportunity to invest in a high-quality asset in one of the country’s most dynamic markets.” CBRE’s Jon Teel represented the buyers in the transaction.
